title: Australia’s $30 billion base boom needs scrutiny too
gist: David Vallance uses satellite imagery to track Australia's nearly $30 billion buildout of four defence sites for the AUKUS era: HMAS Stirling, Osborne, Henderson and RAAF Tindal. Progress is uneven, with Stirling and Tindal well advanced while Henderson's major works have yet to begin and its costs are already estimated at $25 billion over the next decade.

themes.theme: Scale of the defence estate buildout

insights.claim: The Australian government is spending nearly $30 billion across four key defence sites: HMAS Stirling and Henderson in Western Australia, Osborne in South Australia, and RAAF Tindal in the Northern Territory.
insights.speaker: David Vallance
insights.so_what: A multi-decade, $30 billion pipeline of defence construction and engineering work in Australia.
insights.quote: The government is spending nearly $30 billion across four key sites
insights.locator: The government is spending nearly $30 billion

insights.claim: Vallance argues base infrastructure is as crucial to Australia's 'deter, shape, respond' objectives as its expanding navy and guided weapons enterprise, because expensive weapons platforms need homes to be maintained and sustained.
insights.speaker: David Vallance
insights.so_what: Infrastructure is a less-visible but essential leg of defence spending for contractors.
insights.quote: Infrastructure might not seem that exciting. But these expensive weapons all need homes to go to.
insights.locator: Infrastructure might not seem that exciting

insights.claim: Given the money involved, Vallance argues Australia's defence infrastructure projects require scrutiny, not only its submarine and aircraft programs.
insights.speaker: David Vallance
insights.so_what: Heightened oversight may affect cost control and timelines for defence infrastructure contracts.
insights.quote: Given the amount of money involved in improving Australia’s defence infrastructure, these projects also require scrutiny.
insights.locator: How these installations grow and develop

themes.theme: HMAS Stirling and nuclear submarine rotations

insights.claim: HMAS Stirling will host US and then UK nuclear-powered submarines from 2027 as part of Submarine Rotational Force-West, backed by an $8 billion government investment.
insights.speaker: David Vallance
insights.so_what: Near-term AUKUS milestone underpinning Western Australian defence spending.
insights.locator: HMAS Stirling, otherwise known as Fleet Base West

insights.claim: Since AUKUS was announced in 2021, Oxley Wharf at HMAS Stirling has been extended, Diamantia Wharf is to be upgraded for nuclear-powered boats, and a Parkes Wharf extension has apparently been shelved.
insights.speaker: David Vallance
insights.so_what: Scope changes such as shelved works hint at reprioritisation within the base budget.

insights.claim: Shore facilities at HMAS Stirling have been expanded to accommodate about 1000 US military personnel moving to the base.
insights.speaker: David Vallance
insights.so_what: A growing permanent US presence deepens alliance integration and local economic activity.

insights.claim: The Osborne submarine yards in South Australia, central to Australia's ambition to build its own nuclear submarines by the 2040s, have received $8.5 billion of government investment.
insights.speaker: David Vallance
insights.so_what: Sovereign submarine construction is a major cash injection for Australia's defence industry.
insights.locator: AUKUS is not just about military bases

insights.claim: Osborne's Areas 1, 2 and 3 are estimated for completion around 2035, 2036 and 2039 respectively, with the skills campus opening to students in 2028 and Area 3 construction starting next year.
insights.speaker: David Vallance
insights.so_what: Long-dated build schedule implies sustained construction demand through the late 2030s and execution risk.
insights.quote: Areas 1, 2, and 3 are estimated for completion in around 2035, 2036, and 2039 respectively
insights.locator: Works at the site commenced in 2023

themes.theme: Henderson precinct lag and cost escalation

insights.claim: Australia is investing more than $12 billion in the Henderson Defence Precinct for continuous shipbuilding and sustainment including nuclear-powered submarines, but estimates already suggest costs will reach $25 billion over the next decade.
insights.speaker: David Vallance
insights.so_what: Cost estimates already roughly double the headline figure, flagging overrun risk.
insights.quote: Estimates are already suggesting costs will reach $25 billion
insights.locator: The Henderson Defence Precinct south of Perth

insights.claim: Major AUKUS construction at Henderson has yet to commence, with precinct boundaries only decided in August 2026, so major works could begin next year.
insights.speaker: David Vallance
insights.so_what: Major contract awards at Henderson may be imminent.
insights.locator: The Henderson Defence Precinct south of Perth

insights.claim: If Australia is to receive its first nuclear-powered submarine by the early 2030s, construction of the Henderson sustainment facility must proceed at pace.
insights.speaker: David Vallance
insights.so_what: Henderson is a schedule bottleneck for the AUKUS submarine timeline.
insights.locator: The Henderson Defence Precinct south of Perth

themes.theme: Air bases and US force integration

insights.claim: Since 2020, $1.6 billion has been invested at RAAF Tindal to lengthen the runway, expand fuel and munitions storage, and build new hangars and command and control infrastructure.
insights.speaker: David Vallance
insights.so_what: Northern air base hardening is a growing segment of Australian defence spending.
insights.locator: RAAF Tindal in the Northern Territory

insights.claim: RAAF Tindal now hosts Australia's growing fleet of Triton maritime surveillance drones and has runways long enough to land American B-52 bombers.
insights.speaker: David Vallance
insights.so_what: Tindal is becoming a forward node for US power projection in the Indo-Pacific.
insights.locator: RAAF Tindal in the Northern Territory

insights.claim: Talks between Defence Minister Richard Marles and US Secretary of Defence Pete Hegseth emphasised a need to 'swiftly' invest in Australian air force bases, signalling facilities like Tindal will grow in importance.
insights.speaker: David Vallance
insights.so_what: Further air base investment is likely, adding to the defence infrastructure pipeline.

insights.claim: Canberra's impulse to further integrate its defence with Washington goes beyond undersea warfare, with air bases upgraded to host American forces.
insights.speaker: David Vallance
insights.so_what: Deepening US-Australia force integration extends beyond AUKUS submarines.
insights.quote: Canberra’s impulse to further integrate its defence with Washington goes beyond undersea warfare.
